title: AI Use Case Spotting and Automation Discovery

questions.question: Why should AI Use Case Spotting and Automation Discovery be taught as a workflow instead of only as tool awareness?
options: Because brainstorming even more ideas always produces more shippable use cases
Because excitement in a workshop is by itself evidence that a use case will succeed
Because teams need shared signals, controls, and decision rules they can apply to real work
Because any workflow that happens to mention text is automatically a good candidate AI use case
questions.explanation: The lesson is built around reusable operating artifacts — not the idea that more brainstormed ideas ship themselves, that workshop excitement is evidence, or that mentioning text alone qualifies a use case.

questions.question: In the lesson's opening example, why did none of the sixty workshop ideas ship three months later?
options: The workshop simply ran out of time before every one of the sixty ideas could be scored
No one separated attractive-sounding ideas from viable use cases with real pain, data, and a value hypothesis
Leadership rejected the entire sixty-idea backlog outright, citing budget constraints for the whole program
The ideas were technically sound but the team lacked the API access needed to build any of them
questions.explanation: The lesson's opening example ships nothing because the sixty ideas were never separated into viable use cases — ones with real pain, data, repeatability, and a value hypothesis — not because of a time crunch, a budget rejection, or missing API access.

questions.question: What does the Python artifact produce for AI Use Case Spotting and Automation Discovery?
options: A ranked plan with category, score, priority, controls, and rationale
A finished automation script that is ready to deploy without a pilot
A single yes/no verdict on whether a given idea is worth pursuing at all
A slide summarizing every workshop idea for the steering committee
questions.explanation: The lesson's Python artifact outputs a ranked plan — category, score, priority, controls, and rationale — not a ready-to-deploy script, a flat yes/no verdict, or a steering-committee slide.

questions.question: Which control belongs to the lesson design?
options: Assuming a repeatable-sounding workflow needs no data-readiness check before a pilot
Skipping the owner signoff because everyone in the workshop had already agreed on it
Treating the workshop's enthusiasm as the risk review that the idea still has not had
A pilot metric, so the team has a measurable value hypothesis before spending budget
questions.explanation: The lesson's controls include a pilot metric — a measurable value hypothesis before committing budget — the opposite of skipping the data-readiness check, the owner signoff, or the risk review.

questions.question: When should a scenario become a launch-gate discussion rather than a casual awareness exercise?
options: When impact, uncertainty, and matched risk signals such as measurable pain are all high
Only when the use case happens to involve a customer-facing chatbot interface of some kind
Only when more than sixty competing ideas came out of one and the same discovery workshop
Never — a promising use case can always wait until the next portfolio review comes around
questions.explanation: High-impact, uncertain, risk-heavy use cases need a launch gate regardless of the interface, how many ideas competed for attention, or whether a review is already scheduled.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of the output template?
options: To formally replace the portfolio owner's decision about what gets funded next
To keep the workshop's low-scoring ideas hidden from the rest of the group entirely
To create a reusable worksheet or prompt teams keep applying after the course ends
To automatically generate completion certificates once the workshop has ended
questions.explanation: The output template is meant to become a reusable worksheet or prompt teams keep applying — not a substitute for the portfolio owner's funding call, a way to hide low scores, or an automatic certificate generator.
